bull_thesis:
State the conclusion first: the takeover this position was built on is gone, so the bull case is no longer a spread to a contracted price. It is now a bet that Allied Gold is a genuinely cheap gold producer whose biggest asset has not yet started.

The facts that support it are real and recent. On 29 July 2026 Zijin Gold walked away from buying the whole company at C$44.00 a share in cash, but on the same day it agreed to put US$295 million of new money in, subscribing for about 12.8 million shares at C$32.55 each for roughly 9.2% of the company, with rights to top up its stake later. That subscription price is about 28% above where the shares trade today at US$18.23. A buyer who has spent months in the data room chose to invest rather than leave, and Allied's Chairman and Chief Executive and its Vice Chairman voluntarily locked up their own shares alongside it. That closing is expected on or about 10 August 2026 and needs only routine Toronto and New York exchange consents.

Operationally the company is delivering. It produced 97,429 ounces of gold in the second quarter, up about 7% on the same quarter of 2025, and 193,445 ounces in the first half, tracking full-year guidance of 385,000 to 425,000 ounces from the existing mines. All-in sustaining cost, the industry's fully loaded cash cost per ounce sold, is expected to be below US$2,200 against a realized gold price of roughly US$4,380 an ounce, leaving a cash margin over US$2,100 per ounce. Reserves at Agbaou rose more than 60% over the 2025 year-end estimate, lifting that mine's life to 2030, and the Cote d'Ivoire complex now underwrites at least 200,000 ounces a year for more than ten years, raised from 180,000.

The step-change is Kurmuk in Ethiopia. Management says operations start in August 2026 with first gold a few weeks later, on budget and on schedule, and guides Kurmuk to 240,000 to 270,000 ounces in 2027 and roughly 300,000 ounces in 2028 at what it calls industry-leading costs. Adding that to the existing mines takes the company toward roughly 650,000 to 690,000 ounces a year in 2027, from a first-half rate near 390,000 annualized. Pro-forma for the Zijin money, cash is about US$485 million against roughly US$248 million of debt, so the balance sheet carries net cash of about US$237 million and no long-term borrowings.

For this to work, three conditions must hold: Kurmuk must start on time and ramp without a metallurgical surprise; the gold price must stay near current levels long enough for two or three quarters of visible cash generation; and Mali must leave Sadiola alone. If all three hold, a re-rating toward the mid-twenties needs no takeover at all. If Beijing's posture on large outbound acquisitions later softens, Zijin's 9.2% stake and top-up rights make it the obvious renewed bidder, and C$44 is the anchor it has already accepted.
bear_thesis:
The bear case starts from what already happened rather than what might. The event failed. On 29 July 2026 the two companies terminated the arrangement agreement, stating there was no reasonable likelihood the closing conditions would be satisfied by the 29 July outside date or within any reasonable time after it, and they agreed not to extend again. The cause was described as broader external factors applicable to cross-border transactions of this scale, meaning the Chinese approval never arrived. The shares fell 18.3% in one session, from US$20.84 to US$17.03. There is no break fee payable to Allied, so the structural floor that normally bounds a broken deal does not exist here.

Strip out the takeover and what is left has been losing money at record gold prices. Over the trailing twelve months to 31 March 2026 the company earned about US$1.37 billion of revenue and roughly US$301 million of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and US$210 million of pre-tax income, yet a US$290 million income-tax charge produced a net loss of about US$124 million, or US$1.05 a share. That is the eighth consecutive quarterly loss. Cash margins per ounce look outstanding; almost none of it reaches the bottom line, because African tax regimes, state free-carried interests and minority partners take the difference. Any valuation built on cash cost margin rather than on money that actually reaches a shareholder is overstating this business.

Jurisdiction is the deeper problem. Sadiola in Mali produced 92,184 ounces in the first half, roughly 48% of group output, in a country whose 2023 mining code has already been used against a peer major, with gold stock seized and staff detained. Management devoted a section of the 29 July release to rebutting media commentary about security matters in host nations, insisting they are effectively managed and that operations continue without interruption. Companies do not write those paragraphs when nothing is being said. A Mali action would remove nearly half of current production and most of the perceived floor.

Cash is also tighter than the headline suggests. The balance fell from US$425.6 million at 31 March to about US$190 million at 30 June, consumed by Kurmuk capital, tax payments and working capital, a US$236 million drain in a single quarter. The Zijin money refills it, but that is a 9.2% dilution and it is being spent on commissioning a new mine in Ethiopia. Kurmuk has not yet poured an ounce; the 2026 contribution guidance of 100,000 to 150,000 ounces is already being withdrawn for restatement once operations begin.

Finally, ownership has turned over violently. Merger arbitrage funds, who bought a contracted payout, are sellers of an operating gold miner; the 3.9 million shares traded on 31 July against a 696,000-share average is that handover in progress. What confirms the bear case: a Kurmuk commissioning slip past September, a gold price below roughly US$3,600, or any Malian administrative action at Sadiola. Any one of those takes the shares to the low teens, and there is nothing contractual to stop it.
sop_bull:
Event-win value of about US$31.50 a share, which is the terminated Zijin price of C$44.00 converted at the current exchange rate of roughly 1.395 Canadian dollars to the US dollar. This is no longer reachable through the original agreement, which was terminated on 29 July 2026; it is reachable only two ways. Either Zijin, which now owns 9.2% with top-up rights and has already accepted C$44 as fair, returns with a renewed offer once Chinese outbound-transaction policy allows, or the company delivers Kurmuk and re-rates to a normal multiple on its own.

Built from the parts, on 2027 as the first full year with Kurmuk: existing mines roughly 400,000 to 420,000 ounces at an all-in sustaining cost near US$2,100 an ounce, plus Kurmuk at 240,000 to 270,000 ounces at a materially lower cost, call it US$1,250. That is about 660,000 ounces at a blended cost near US$1,780. At a US$4,380 gold price the cash margin is roughly US$2,600 an ounce, or about US$1.7 billion, less around US$80 million of corporate overhead and exploration outside the cost measure and roughly US$45 million of interest, leaving about US$1.6 billion of pre-tax operating earnings. Capitalising that at 2.5 times, a deeply discounted multiple that reflects West African political risk, gives an enterprise value of about US$4.0 billion. Adding pro-forma net cash of about US$237 million and dividing by the 139.3 million shares outstanding after the Zijin placement gives roughly US$30.50 a share. The C$44 anchor and this build agree at about US$31. Contributions: existing Cote d'Ivoire and Mali mines about US$17, Kurmuk about US$12, net cash about US$1.70.
sop_bear:
Verified downside floor of about US$13.00 a share. Our board carried US$17, but that figure is simply where the shares closed on the day the deal broke, not a floor with anything behind it. There is no break fee and no cash election, so the only genuine backstop is the asset base at a stressed gold price with the Mali risk realised.

The build: assume Sadiola, 92,184 ounces in the first half and about 48% of production, is heavily impaired under a Malian administrative action of the kind a peer major has already suffered. What remains is the Cote d'Ivoire complex at roughly 200,000 ounces a year and Kurmuk at roughly 250,000 ounces, about 450,000 ounces at a blended all-in sustaining cost near US$1,700. At a stressed gold price of US$3,800 an ounce that is a cash margin of about US$945 million, which after the local tax take, state free-carried interests and minority partners leaves roughly US$450 million attributable. Capitalising at 3.5 times gives about US$1.58 billion of enterprise value, plus pro-forma net cash of about US$237 million, or US$1.82 billion of equity across 139.3 million shares, which is about US$13.05 a share.

Contributions in this case: Cote d'Ivoire complex about US$7.50, Kurmuk about US$3.80, net cash about US$1.70, Mali written to zero. Note that this floor is an estimate of value, not a contractual minimum, and it would break further if gold fell below roughly US$3,400 or Kurmuk's ramp disappointed.
sop_breakdown:
Base case is a probability weighting of three outcomes, not a single model. A renewed control transaction at roughly US$31.50 carries about a 20% chance: Zijin holds 9.2% with top-up rights and has already accepted C$44, but the blocking factor is geopolitical, outside either party's control, and both companies stated on record that conditions would not be met within any reasonable time. A standalone re-rating to about US$26 carries about 55%, and requires only that Kurmuk starts as guided in August 2026 and that two or three quarters of visible cash generation arrive at a gold price near US$4,380. A stress case at about US$13.00 carries about 25%, driven by Malian action at Sadiola or a gold price retreat. That weighting gives 0.20 x 31.50 plus 0.55 x 26.00 plus 0.25 x 13.00, or about US$23.85, which we round to US$23.50.

The cross-check is reassuring: Zijin is subscribing at C$32.55, about US$23.33 at 1.395, which sits almost exactly on this base case. A strategic buyer with full diligence access is writing a cheque at our reconciled fair value.

Parts contributing to the base case, per share on the 139.3 million shares outstanding after the placement: Cote d'Ivoire complex (Bonikro and Agbaou, 101,261 ounces in the first half, reserves extended to 2030) about US$9.00; Sadiola in Mali (92,184 ounces in the first half, carried at a heavy political discount) about US$5.50; Kurmuk in Ethiopia (starting August 2026, guided to 240,000 to 270,000 ounces in 2027) about US$7.30; pro-forma net cash of roughly US$237 million about US$1.70. Total about US$23.50.
risk_reward:
Roughly one to one on the base case, and about two and a half to one measuring the best case against the floor. From US$18.23 the upside to the reconciled fair value of US$23.50 is about 29%; the downside to the verified floor of US$13.00 is about 29%. Measuring instead to the renewed-bid case of US$31.50 gives 73% up against 29% down, or about 2.5 to 1, but that outcome carries only about a 20% probability and no date.

This is materially worse than the 1.27 our board carried, and for a specific reason: that figure was computed against a US$31.50 target that was a contracted cash price and a US$17.00 floor. As of 29 July 2026 the contract is void, so the target is now a hope rather than a claim, and US$17 was never a floor at all, merely the closing price on the day the deal broke. Adjusting both inputs to what can actually be verified takes the asymmetry from attractive to ordinary.
catalyst_summary: The takeover fired and failed: Allied Gold and Zijin Gold terminated their C$44.00-a-share cash arrangement on 29 July 2026 when Chinese cross-border approval never came, and the shares fell 18.3% in a day; what replaces it is a US$295 million Zijin minority investment at C$32.55 closing about 10 August 2026 and first gold at Kurmuk in Ethiopia within weeks, leaving roughly 29% upside to a US$23.50 fair value against 29% downside to a US$13.00 floor that nothing contractual protects.
dated_milestone: 29 July 2026: arrangement agreement terminated, outside date not extended (verified in Allied Gold's Form 6-K filed 29 July 2026, Exhibit 99.1). On or about 10 August 2026: Zijin Gold's US$295 million subscription for about 12.8 million shares at C$32.55, roughly 9.2% of the company, is expected to close, subject only to Toronto Stock Exchange and New York Stock Exchange approval. August 2026: Kurmuk mine start of operations, with first gold a few weeks thereafter, on budget and on schedule per the same filing. Second-half 2026 production guidance to be restated once Kurmuk operations commence.
forcing_function:
The transactional catalyst is spent, so the only thing left that can force a re-rating is operational: first gold at Kurmuk, guided for August 2026 with pour a few weeks after start-up, followed by the restated second-half guidance the company has promised once operations commence. Kurmuk is guided to 240,000 to 270,000 ounces in 2027 and roughly 300,000 ounces in 2028 at industry-leading costs, against 193,445 ounces for the entire company in the first half of 2026. If it starts on time and the first two quarters of consolidated cash flow show the blended cost falling as promised, the market has to price a company producing well over 600,000 ounces rather than under 400,000.

A secondary and much smaller trigger is the 10 August 2026 closing of Zijin's US$295 million subscription. It puts a fresh, publicly disclosed strategic price of C$32.55 on the shares, roughly 28% above the market, and removes any financing question over the Kurmuk ramp. It pays existing holders nothing directly.

There is no date behind the outcome that would matter most, a renewed Zijin offer. Both companies stated on 29 July that the conditions would not be satisfied within any reasonable time, and the obstacle is Chinese policy toward large cross-border acquisitions, which neither company controls. Assigning that a date would be invention.
consensus_delta:
The market and this position were both wrong, in opposite directions, and only one of them has corrected. Through July the shares traded around US$20.85 while the contracted price was about US$31.50, implying the market gave the deal roughly a five-in-a-hundred chance of closing. Our board still carried the full US$31.50 as the target and US$17.00 as the floor. The market was right and it has now been proved right: the agreement was terminated on 29 July 2026.

Where a genuine disagreement remains is on what the company is worth without the deal. The market is marking the shares at US$18.23. Zijin, which spent months inside the data room, is subscribing at C$32.55, about US$23.33, for a 9.2% stake it cannot sell for four months and a day. Those two prices cannot both be right. Our read is that the selling is mechanical rather than informed: merger arbitrage funds bought a contracted payout and are now holding an operating African gold miner they were never mandated to own, and the 3.9 million shares that traded on 31 July against a 696,000-share average is that handover.

The second disagreement is on earnings quality, and here we side with the sceptics rather than the bulls. Management leads with a cash cost below US$2,200 an ounce against a realized gold price near US$4,380, which sounds like an enormous margin. But over the trailing twelve months the company turned US$210 million of pre-tax income into a US$124 million net loss because of a US$290 million tax charge, the eighth consecutive quarterly loss. Anyone valuing this on cost margin per ounce rather than on cash that actually reaches a shareholder is making the same error twice over. The correct disagreement to hold is narrow: the shares are probably too cheap against a strategic's own fresh cheque, but nowhere near as cheap as the operating margins make them look.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry three specific hazards, and the position has no contractual protection against any of them.

First, the cash trough is real and only just being refilled. Cash fell from US$425.6 million at 31 March 2026 to about US$190 million at 30 June, a US$236 million drain in one quarter, consumed by Kurmuk construction capital, normal-course tax payments and working capital. The company is commissioning a new mine on a thinner balance sheet than at any point this year. The US$295 million from Zijin, expected on or about 10 August, restores it to roughly US$485 million against about US$248 million of debt, but until that closes there is no buffer, and the money is earmarked for the Kurmuk ramp, the Sadiola expansion and Cote d'Ivoire production increases rather than for shareholders.

Second, commissioning risk. Kurmuk is guided to start in August with first gold a few weeks later. New mines slip; metallurgy disappoints; ramp curves stretch. Management has already said it will restate the 2026 contribution, previously 100,000 to 150,000 ounces, once operations commence, which is an honest signal that the number is uncertain. A slip past September would leave the company with a spent balance sheet, no new production and no deal.

Third, and most severe, Mali. Sadiola is roughly 48% of current output and sits under a 2023 mining code that has already been used against a peer major, with gold stock seized and executives detained. Allied felt it necessary on 29 July to publish a rebuttal of media commentary on security matters in its host nations, asserting that they are effectively managed and that operations continue without interruption. That may be entirely true, and the operating record supports it, but the need to say it at all is the risk. A Malian administrative action would remove half the production base in a single announcement.

Behind all three sits the gold price. At roughly US$4,380 an ounce the cash margins are extraordinary. The entire floor in this analysis assumes gold no lower than about US$3,800. Below roughly US$3,400 the floor does not hold.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling is happening now and is the clearest short-term feature of the tape. A merger arbitrage shareholder base bought one thing, a contracted C$44.00 cash payout with a defined date, and on 29 July was handed something else entirely, an equity position in a mid-tier African gold producer. Most such funds have mandates that do not permit holding it, so the selling is mechanical rather than a judgement about value.

The evidence is in the volumes. Against an average of about 696,000 shares a day, 3.19 million traded on 29 July as the shares fell 18.3% to US$17.03, then 927,900 on 30 July, then 3.90 million on 31 July as the price recovered to US$18.23. Heavy volume with a rising price on the third day is the signature of a handover: arbitrage sellers meeting value buyers, rather than a one-way liquidation.

Two things cushion it. Zijin's 12.8 million subscription shares are locked for four months and a day under Canadian rules, and the Chairman and Chief Executive and the Vice Chairman voluntarily matched that lock-up. So roughly 9.2% of the enlarged register plus the largest insider holdings are immobilised into December 2026. That removes supply rather than adding it.

The offsetting risk is index and rating flow. The shares were added to a strong-sell screen on 21 July, and a busted transaction typically triggers a round of estimate withdrawals and coverage resets. Expect the arbitrage exit to be substantially complete within a few weeks, but do not expect a natural long-only buyer base to form until Kurmuk has actually poured gold.
moderator_conclusion:
The honest verdict is that this seat no longer holds the investment it was underwritten for. Allied Gold came into the book as a merger arbitrage: a contracted C$44.00-a-share cash price, roughly US$31.50, with a hard outside date and what looked like a bounded loss. On 29 July 2026 both companies terminated the agreement, stating there was no reasonable likelihood the conditions would be met by the deadline or within any reasonable time after it, and agreed not to extend. The cause was Chinese approval for a cross-border deal of that size, which never came. The shares fell 18.3% in a session. There is no break fee payable to Allied. The spread did not narrow; it ceased to exist, and no amount of residual quality changes that this particular event has resolved and resolved badly.

What is left is a genuinely interesting company that belongs in a different lane. Zijin walked from the takeover but immediately committed US$295 million for 9.2% at C$32.55 a share, roughly US$23.33 and about 28% above today's price, closing on or about 10 August with only routine exchange consents outstanding, and it took top-up rights to stay pro-rata. Allied's own Chairman and Chief Executive and its Vice Chairman locked up their shares beside it. Operationally the company is executing: 97,429 ounces in the second quarter, up 7% year on year; 193,445 ounces in the first half against 385,000 to 425,000 ounces of full-year guidance; cash costs below US$2,200 against a realized gold price near US$4,380; Agbaou reserves up more than 60%. And Kurmuk, the Ethiopian mine that roughly doubles the growth profile, starts within weeks, on budget and on schedule.

Against that sit two facts that keep us honest. The company has now posted eight consecutive quarterly losses at record gold prices, because a US$290 million tax charge on US$210 million of pre-tax income is what African operation costs; the cash margin per ounce is not the shareholder's margin. And nearly half of current production sits in Mali, under a mining code already used against a peer major, in a country where the company found it necessary to publicly rebut commentary about security. That is why our floor is US$13.00 rather than the US$17.00 the board carried, which was only the closing price on the day the deal broke, with nothing behind it.

Reconciling the parts gives a base-case value of about US$23.50 a share, which lands almost exactly on Zijin's own subscription price of US$23.33, a satisfying cross-check from a buyer with full diligence access. From US$18.23 that is 29% up against 29% down to the floor, roughly one to one. For a dated-event sleeve that is not enough. Pass for now, and retire the seat. If the residual value case is wanted, and there is a real one, it should be re-underwritten as an operating gold producer with a first-gold catalyst in August, not carried forward as a spread that no longer exists.
interrogator_dossier:
# Allied Gold Corporation (AAUC) — Forensic Dossier on the Event

*Prepared 3 August 2026. All facts below are sourced to filings with the U.S. Securities and
Exchange Commission (SEC) or company press releases, with dates given.*

## The headline finding, stated plainly

**The takeover is dead.** On 29 July 2026 Allied Gold and Zijin Gold International jointly
terminated the arrangement agreement under which Zijin was to buy all of Allied for C$44.00 a
share in cash — roughly US$31.50, which is exactly the target price our board was carrying. The
two companies concluded there was "no reasonable likelihood that the conditions relating to
completion of the Transaction will be fulfilled by the outside date of July 29, 2026 or within
any reasonable time thereafter," and mutually agreed **not** to extend the deadline again. The
stated cause was "broader external factors applicable to cross-border transactions of this
scale" — the polite formulation for the Chinese outbound-investment approval that never came.

The merger-arbitrage spread this position was built on no longer exists. It did not narrow; it
vanished. Any analysis that still treats US$31.50 as a reachable, contractual payout is working
from a stale board.

**Source:** Allied Gold Corp, Form 6-K filed 29 July 2026, Exhibit 99.1 (accession
0001171843-26-004981 / -004980), and the company's release of the same date.

## 1. What actually happened, in sequence

| Date | Event | What it told us at the time |
|---|---|---|
| 29 May 2026 | Zijin receives approval under the Investment Canada Act; Allied announces the Canadian approval process is "complete" and **extends the outside date to 29 July 2026** | Progress on the approval that was never the binding constraint; silence on the one that was |
| 10 June 2026 | Allied states both parties "remain fully committed to fulfilling the conditions for completion... by the extended outside date of July 29, 2026" | A confidence statement seven weeks before the deal died |
| 27 July 2026 | Stock trades at US$20.85; third-party commentary notes the market was pricing roughly a 5% chance of completion | The market had already voted; the company had not updated its language |
| 29 July 2026 | **Arrangement agreement terminated.** Concurrently, Zijin signs a subscription agreement for a US$295 million minority stake | The event resolved — against holders |
| 29 July 2026 | Shares close at US$17.03, down 18.3% from US$20.84 the prior session | The break was repriced in a single day |
| 31 July 2026 | Shares close at US$18.23 on 3.9 million shares (roughly 5.6x the 696,000-share average) | Partial recovery on heavy volume — arbitrage funds exiting, value buyers arriving |

### The consolation prize, and what it is worth

Zijin did not simply walk away. On the same day it agreed to subscribe, through a non-brokered
private placement, for approximately **12.8 million Allied common shares at C$32.55 each**, for
gross proceeds of roughly **US$295 million (about C$417 million)**, leaving it with about
**9.2%** of the company. Three details matter:

- **The price is a real, third-party mark, but a backward-looking one.** C$32.55 is stated in
  the filing to be the 30-day volume-weighted average price on the Toronto exchange as of 27
  July 2026 — a mechanical formula struck before the break, not an independent valuation. It
  now sits roughly **28% above** where the shares trade (C$32.55 ≈ US$23.33 versus US$18.23).
- **It is a dated, near-term event.** Closing is "expected to occur on or about **10 August
  2026**," subject only to Toronto Stock Exchange and New York Stock Exchange approval. Those
  are administrative consents, not discretionary ones.
- **It pays common holders nothing.** This is a capital raise, not an exit. It dilutes existing
  holders by about 9.2% at a price above market — which raises net asset value per share
  modestly — and hands the company US$295 million of cash. Zijin gets participation and top-up
  rights to hold its pro-rata stake, and the shares carry a four-month-and-a-day Canadian hold
  period. Allied's Chairman and Chief Executive and its Vice Chairman voluntarily locked up
  their own shares for the same window.

**No termination fee is disclosed as payable to Allied.** The termination was mutual and by its
terms, so the usual break-fee backstop that bounds a busted-deal position is absent here.

## 2. Is there still a real, dated, binding catalyst?

Only in a much smaller sense, and it is operational rather than transactional.

- **Binding and dated (low value):** the 10 August 2026 closing of the US$295 million placement.
  Near-certain, but it is a financing, not a re-rating event.
- **Dated but not binding (high value):** **Kurmuk**. Allied's new Ethiopian mine is guided to
  "start of operations expected in August and first gold following a few weeks thereafter,"
  on budget and on schedule, per the 29 July release. This is the genuine forcing function.
  Kurmuk is guided to produce 240,000–270,000 ounces in 2027 and roughly 300,000 ounces in 2028
  at what management calls industry-leading costs — a step-change against 193,445 ounces
  produced across the whole company in the first half of 2026.
- **Undated and speculative:** a renewed Zijin bid. Zijin now holds a 9.2% foothold with top-up
  rights and has demonstrated it wants the asset at C$44. But the obstacle that killed the deal
  is geopolitical and outside either company's control, and both sides went out of their way to
  say the conditions would not be met "within any reasonable time." Assigning this a date would
  be fabrication.

## 3. Management credibility — split verdict

**Operationally, they have delivered.** Second-quarter production of 97,429 ounces was up 7%
against the same quarter of 2025 and in line with plan; first-half production of 193,445 ounces
tracks the 385,000–425,000-ounce full-year guidance for the producing mines. All-in sustaining
cost — the industry's fully loaded cash cost per ounce sold — is expected to come in below
US$2,200 for the quarter against a realized gold price of roughly US$4,380 an ounce, a margin of
more than US$2,100 per ounce. Reserves at Agbaou rose more than 60% over the 2025 year-end
estimate, extending that mine's life to 2030, and Bonikro's life was previously extended. That
is a credible operating record.

**On the transaction, the communication was one-sided.** Allied publicised the approval it had
obtained (Canada, 29 May) and reiterated commitment to the 29 July deadline as late as 10 June,
while the approval it actually needed remained unresolved. That is not misrepresentation — the
Chinese decision was not Allied's to make or to disclose — but investors reading only the
company's releases would have been materially more optimistic than the market was. Anyone sizing
this position off management's tone rather than the tape was hurt.

**A related governance tell:** on 30 July, one day after the break, Allied filed an update
conceding that during the deal "it was initially determined that a shareholder meeting would not
be required given the expectation of a closing of the transaction beforehand," and that board
refreshment discussions were not possible. The company has now committed to nominating at least
20% women to the board at the 2027 annual meeting and 30% at the 2028 meeting. In plain terms:
the pending sale was used as a reason to defer normal shareholder governance for a half-year,
and that deferral is only now being unwound.

## 4. The verified downside floor — and why it is softer than the board assumed

Our board carried a floor of US$17. That number is the post-break trading print (the 29 July
close was US$17.03), not a floor in any structural sense. There is no cash-election, no break
fee, and no collateral behind it. What genuinely backstops the price is the operating asset base
and the balance sheet:

- **Balance sheet (hard).** Cash was approximately US$190 million at 30 June 2026, down from
  US$425.6 million at 31 March, drained by Kurmuk construction capital, tax payments and working
  capital. Adding the US$295 million placement takes pro-forma cash to roughly US$485 million
  against about US$248 million of total debt — net cash of roughly US$237 million, or about
  US$1.70 a share on the 139.3 million shares outstanding after the placement. That is real, but
  it is 9% of the share price, not a floor.
- **Producing asset base (soft).** Three producing mines plus Kurmuk. The floor is whatever the
  market will pay for those cash flows at a stressed gold price — and, critically, at whatever
  jurisdictional discount it chooses to apply.

**The floor's real weakness is Mali.** Sadiola produced 92,184 ounces in the first half, about
48% of group output, and sits in a jurisdiction where a peer major saw its gold stock seized and
staff detained under the 2023 mining code. A stress case in which Sadiola's value is heavily
impaired, leaving the Côte d'Ivoire complex and Kurmuk, supports something closer to **US$13**
per share than US$17. That is the honest floor. Note also that management felt compelled to
devote a section of the 29 July release to "Addressing Certain Commentary Related to Security
Matters in Host Nations," stating that such matters "have been, and continue to be, effectively
managed" and that operations continue "without interruption to supply chains or otherwise." A
company that must publicly rebut security commentary is a company whose floor carries a
political discount, whether or not the rebuttal is accurate.

## 5. Red flags

- 🔴 **The load-bearing event failed.** Not delayed — terminated by mutual agreement, with both
  parties on record that it will not be revived "within any reasonable time."
- 🔴 **No break fee to Allied.** The defined-risk structure that normally bounds a broken
  arbitrage position is simply absent.
- 🔴 **Eight straight quarters of bottom-line losses at record gold prices.** Trailing
  twelve-month revenue of about US$1.37 billion produced roughly US$301 million of earnings
  before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation and US$210 million of pre-tax income — but
  a US$290 million income-tax charge turned that into a US$124 million net loss, or US$1.05 per

  sustaining cost margin" and money that reaches a shareholder is the single most important

- 🔴 **A one-day 18% drawdown on a scheduled deadline.** The market knew; the company's own

## 6. Green flags

- 🟢 **A sophisticated strategic is buying, not leaving.** Zijin is putting US$295 million of new

- 🟢 **Insider alignment:** the Chairman/Chief Executive and Vice Chairman voluntarily locked up

- 🟢 **Pro-forma net cash** of roughly US$237 million, with no long-term debt on the balance sheet.

## 7. What the director must weigh

This name entered the book as a merger arbitrage with a contractual payout and a bounded loss.
It is now neither. What remains is a mid-tier African gold producer, trading at roughly US$18.23
against a strategic investor's fresh US$23.33-equivalent subscription price, with a new mine
starting in weeks and a very large, very real political discount attached to nearly half its
current production.

That may well be a good investment. **It is not the investment this seat was underwritten for,
and it carries no floor worth the name.** The correct action for a dated-event sleeve is to
retire the position and, if the residual value case is wanted, re-underwrite it in a lane built
for operating companies rather than for spreads.
